disagreements.researcher_position: A deed of partition affects immovable property and is therefore governed by section 2(1) of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, so notarial execution is a condition of its validity.
disagreements.verifier_position: Section 2(1) is expressed by reference to sale, purchase, transfer, assignment or mortgage and to promises, bargains, contracts or agreements for effecting such an object or establishing an interest affecting land. It does not name partition, and two other statutes in the corpus treat a deed of partition of land held in common as something other than a transfer. The proposition is probably right in practice but is not read off the section, and it is the premise of the whole answer.

disagreements.researcher_position: Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 s.2 gives a third route: the Tangalle party may execute before the District Judge for her district, and the corpus records no repeal.
disagreements.verifier_position: Two separate doubts. The section is keyed to a District Judge or Commissioner of a Court of Requests, an office abolished by court-structure legislation outside this corpus, and the section speaks of the deed being signed before the officer, saying nothing about one of four parties doing so while the others execute before notaries. Marked unresolved rather than rejected.

disagreements.researcher_position: Rule (27)(c)(ii) puts a three-month outer limit on the staggered-signing route, so the deed should be completed within three months of the first signature.
disagreements.verifier_position: The rule imposes no deadline. It obliges the notary, if called upon by written notice from the Registrar of Lands, to deliver the duplicate, and entitles him to demand it back within the following two years for the purpose of completing the deed. The advice is prudent but is presented as a statutory limit.

lawyer_questions: Does a deed of partition between co-owners fall within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance? Everything in this answer, including the third route, is built on that premise, and the section's words do not say so.

Is Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 still in operation after the abolition of the Court of Requests, and if so may one party of four execute before the District Judge while the other three execute before a notary?

Read with the 2022 and 2024 amendments to the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, do the words present at the same time and in the presence of one another attach to each signing event, so that section 32(2) and rule (25) of the Notaries Ordinance still permit two notaries at two sittings?

What is the correct rule number for the paragraph inserted into section 31 after rule (15) requiring an attorney's affidavit? The map cites rule (15A)(c) and the corpus carries the paragraph unnumbered.

Is the practical advice to complete a staggered signing within three months right, given that rule (27)(c)(ii) only triggers a notice-driven duty to deliver the duplicate, returnable within two years for completion?
